text:
**Probably yes, but only if closing costs come in under roughly $10–12k.** A 0.6-point drop on $400k is marginal, so the fees decide it.

**The real savings:** 0.6% × $400k ≈ **$2,400/year in interest**, or about $200/month. That shrinks slowly as the balance falls, so over 10 years you'd save roughly **$21–22k** in interest.

**Breakeven at typical closing costs (2–5% of the loan):**

| Closing costs | Breakeven | Net after 10 years |
|---|---|---|
| $6k | ~2.5 years | ~+$15k |
| $10k | ~4 years | ~+$11k |
| $14k | ~6 years | ~+$7k |
| $18k+ | ~8+ years | roughly a wash |

**Watch for these:**

- **Don't judge by the monthly payment.** If you're a few years into your current loan and refinance into a new 30-year, the payment drops more than the rate alone explains, partly because you've restarted the clock and will pay longer. Compare interest cost, or take a 25-year term to match what you have left, or keep paying your current amount.
- **Get a Loan Estimate from 2–3 lenders** and compare total costs: origination, points, title, appraisal. Ask whether you can get title-insurance reissue rates, which can save a meaningful chunk.
- **Consider a no-cost or lender-credit refi** at maybe ~6.1–6.2%. Less savings, but nothing to recoup, which protects you if you move earlier or rates fall further and you want to refi again.
- **"About 10 years" is doing a lot of work.** If there's a real chance you move in 4–5 years, only a low-cost deal makes sense.

If you get quotes with total costs around $8k or less, it's a clear yes. If they're $15k+, I'd pass or take the no-cost option.
